<!-- slide · waffle theory -->
## Waffle Charts {.smaller}

[Cohort summaries · theory]{.eyebrow}

### Part-to-whole as a grid of squares

A waffle is a 10×10-ish grid where each square is one unit and each colour block is a category, more honest than a pie because you can *count* the squares. Use it for whole-number compositions: variant classifications, cohort cell types, genotype counts.

It works best with a handful of categories that sum to a round total. Here: the outcome of a clinical variant panel, where the punchline is how much grey (VUS) there is.


<!-- slide · waffle data -->
## Waffle · The Data {.smaller}

[Cohort summaries]{.eyebrow}

### Variant interpretations from a panel screen

`load_variant_classes()` is a tiny table: each ACMG category and how many variants fell into it. They sum to 150, a clean number to tile.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
from genomics_course.data import load_variant_classes

vc = load_variant_classes()   # classification, n
vc
```


<!-- slide · waffle step 1 -->
## Waffle · Step 1 — Tile the Counts {.smaller}

[Cohort summaries · build]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · Counts to squares

`PyWaffle` plugs into matplotlib via `FigureClass=Waffle`. Give it `rows` and a `values` dict of category → count; it lays one square per unit, block by block.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "5-9"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 3.6
# pip install pywaffle
from pywaffle import Waffle
from genomics_course.data import load_variant_classes

vc = load_variant_classes()                              # classification, n
pal = [RED, AMBER, GREY, BLUE, GREEN]                    # colour per ACMG class
fig = plt.figure(FigureClass=Waffle, rows=10,            # 10 rows → 15 cols for 150 squares
                 values=dict(zip(vc.classification, vc.n)),  # category → count
                 colors=pal, figsize=(6.6, 3.6),
                 block_aspect_ratio=1)                   # square blocks
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · waffle step 2 -->
## Waffle · Step 2 — Legend & Finding {.smaller}

[Cohort summaries · build]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · Name the categories and the message

Add a legend outside the grid and a title that states the takeaway. The grey expanse needs no explanation: most variants are of uncertain significance.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "10-12"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 3.6
from pywaffle import Waffle
from genomics_course.data import load_variant_classes

vc = load_variant_classes()                              # classification, n
pal = [RED, AMBER, GREY, BLUE, GREEN]                    # colour per ACMG class
fig = plt.figure(FigureClass=Waffle, rows=10,
                 values=dict(zip(vc.classification, vc.n)),
                 colors=pal, figsize=(6.6, 3.6),
                 block_aspect_ratio=1,
                 legend={"loc": "upper left", "bbox_to_anchor": (1, 1),   # key, outside right
                         "fontsize": 8, "frameon": False},
                 title={"label": "Most variants are VUS",                 # title = the finding
                        "fontsize": 12, "fontweight": "bold"})
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
A waffle turns counts into countable squares: **`values` dict → tile → legend → title**. Reach for it over a pie when categories are few and the total is a round number, here, the wall of grey says "VUS dominates" instantly.
:::


<!-- slide · waterfall theory -->
## Waterfall Plots {.smaller}

[Cohort summaries · theory]{.eyebrow}

### A cohort ranked into a skyline

A waterfall is a bar per sample, sorted by the value, so the cohort reads as a descending skyline. It's the staple cancer-genomics view of **tumour mutation burden**: who carries the most mutations, and does a subtype or marker cluster at the top.

The moves: sort descending, colour the bars by a categorical (subtype), and overlay a marker for a second variable (here MSI status) so two facts share one axis.


<!-- slide · waterfall data -->
## Waterfall · The Data {.smaller}

[Cohort summaries]{.eyebrow}

### TMB across a 60-patient cohort

`load_tmb_cohort()` gives one row per patient: their TMB, breast-cancer `subtype`, and microsatellite status (`msi`). MSI-H tumours are biologically hypermutated, we expect them high.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
from genomics_course.data import load_tmb_cohort

co = load_tmb_cohort()   # patient, tmb, subtype, msi
co.head(4)
```


<!-- slide · waterfall step 1 -->
## Waterfall · Step 1 — Rank into Bars {.smaller}

[Cohort summaries · build]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · Sort, then one bar each

Sort by TMB descending and draw a bar per patient with `width=1.0` so they form a continuous skyline. The shape, a steep head and a long tail, is the whole point.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "3,6-7"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.2
from genomics_course.data import load_tmb_cohort

co = load_tmb_cohort().sort_values("tmb", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)  # rank desc

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
ax.bar(range(len(co)), co.tmb, color=GREY, width=1.0, linewidth=0)  # one bar per patient
ax.set_xticks([])                                                  # individual ids aren't useful
ax.set_xlabel("patients (ranked by TMB)"); ax.set_ylabel("TMB (mut/Mb)")
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · waterfall step 2 -->
## Waterfall · Step 2 — Colour by Subtype {.smaller}

[Cohort summaries · build]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · Map a colour to each subtype

Build a subtype → colour dict and map it onto the sorted bars. Now you can scan whether any subtype clusters in the high-TMB head.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "5,9"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.2
from genomics_course.data import load_tmb_cohort

co = load_tmb_cohort().sort_values("tmb", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
sub_pal = {"Luminal A": GREEN, "Luminal B": BLUE,        # one colour per subtype
           "HER2+": AMBER, "TNBC": RED}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
ax.bar(range(len(co)), co.tmb, width=1.0, linewidth=0,
       color=co.subtype.map(sub_pal))                    # colour each bar by its subtype
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("patients (ranked by TMB)"); ax.set_ylabel("TMB (mut/Mb)")
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · waterfall step 3 -->
## Waterfall · Step 3 — Flag MSI-H, Title It {.smaller}

[Cohort summaries · build]{.eyebrow}

### 3 · A second variable, and the finding

Drop a star above each MSI-H patient's bar, build a combined legend (subtype patches + the star), and title with the result. The stars cluster in the head, MSI-H tumours are the hypermutators.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "2,12-14,19-21"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 4.2
from genomics_course.data import load_tmb_cohort
from matplotlib.patches import Patch                     # for the legend swatches

co = load_tmb_cohort().sort_values("tmb", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)
sub_pal = {"Luminal A": GREEN, "Luminal B": BLUE, "HER2+": AMBER, "TNBC": RED}

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.2))
ax.bar(range(len(co)), co.tmb, width=1.0, linewidth=0, color=co.subtype.map(sub_pal))
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("patients (ranked by TMB)"); ax.set_ylabel("TMB (mut/Mb)")
msi = co.msi == "MSI-H"                                   # boolean mask of MSI-H patients
ax.scatter(co.index[msi], co.tmb[msi] + co.tmb.max() * .03,  # a star just above each MSI-H bar
           marker="*", color=INK, s=55, zorder=5)
for s in ["top", "right"]: ax.spines[s].set_visible(False)
ax.set_title("MSI-H TUMOURS ARE HYPERMUTATED", color="#333333", fontweight="bold", loc="left")
handles = [Patch(color=c, label=k) for k, c in sub_pal.items()]      # subtype swatches...
handles += [plt.Line2D([0], [0], marker="*", color=INK, ls="none", label="MSI-H")]  # ...plus the star
ax.legend(handles=handles, frameon=False, fontsize=8, ncol=2)
plt.show()
```

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
A waterfall ranks a cohort into a skyline: **sort descending → colour by subtype → overlay a second variable → title the finding**. Here the MSI-H stars pile up in the high-TMB head, exactly the biology you'd expect.
:::
